title: Building the Article 13 audit trail before the regulator calls
linkedinPost:
4 days into EU AI Act enforcement.

If your AI system routes model calls through a shared service account, you don't have a compliant audit trail.

You have a log that records calls but not who directed them. Under GDPR, DORA, and MiFID II, that's the compliance gap regulators find first.

The Traceability Stack — the 4 layers that make an AI audit trail actually compliant:

• Layer 1 — Event. Every AI operation: input, output, timestamp, model version. Most teams think this is the audit trail. It's only the start.

• Layer 2 — Attribution. The named person (not service account) who directed the call. The most common gap in supervised firms.

• Layer 3 — Context. Prompt version hash, system instructions, data source vintage. Without this, you can't reconstruct what the model was running under when it made the decision.

• Layer 4 — Oversight. Human review, override, escalation — structured, timestamped, with reasoning.

What I would actually do:
• Fix attribution first — reroute service account calls to user-specific tokens within 30 days
• Set up a dedicated ai_decision_log table in EU-sovereign infrastructure
• Add prompt versioning before the next model update
• Run a simulated regulatory review: can you reconstruct a credit decision end-to-end from your logs?

Revenue per employee doesn't move from AI you can't deploy in production. Compliant audit architecture is what keeps it there.

Full piece + the Traceability Stack schema — link in comments.

mainEntity.name: What does EU AI Act Article 13 require for audit trails in financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: Article 13 requires that high-risk AI systems are sufficiently transparent that deployers can interpret the system's outputs and the event logs generated during operation. For financial services firms, this means providers must supply instructions explaining what the Article 12 log captures and how to reconstruct a decision from it. Both the log and the interpretive documentation must be available to national supervisory authorities on request.

mainEntity.name: How long must AI audit logs be retained under the EU AI Act?

acceptedAnswer.text: Article 12 requires deployers of high-risk AI systems to retain logs for a minimum of 6 months. For biometric identification and law enforcement AI systems, the retention period is 24 months. These are minimums — DORA and MiFID II impose additional documentation and retention requirements for financial entities, and firms should apply the longest applicable period across all overlapping regimes.

mainEntity.name: What is the most common AI audit trail compliance gap in financial services?

acceptedAnswer.text: Missing individual attribution. When AI model calls route through a shared service account or API key, the log captures the call but not the person who directed it. GDPR, DORA, and MiFID II all require individual attribution for AI decisions affecting data subjects or financial outcomes. A credit decision with no named human in the log chain has no compliant audit trail regardless of how complete the event record is.

mainEntity.name: What happens if a regulated firm cannot produce an AI audit trail when requested?

acceptedAnswer.text: Under the EU AI Act, failure to maintain compliant documentation for high-risk AI systems carries fines up to €15 million or 3% of global annual revenue, whichever is higher. Under DORA, which applies to all financial entities in the EU from January 2025, failure to maintain adequate ICT risk documentation — which regulators increasingly interpret to include AI decision logs — carries additional supervisory action by competent national authorities including the ECB, EBA, and national NCAs.
